content_html:
No First Cause

“No first cause” rejects an ultimate starting point. It replaces it with conditioned co‑arising (Buddhism), state evolution from prior states (science), and process‑oriented metaphysics (philosophy). Practically, it shifts attention from origins to conditions we can change now.

No first cause means phenomena do not originate from an ultimate, single source. Instead, they arise interdependently from conditions. Buddhism articulates this as dependent origination; science models it via recursive/relational dynamics (networks, initial conditions, symmetry-breaking); philosophy contrasts this with traditions that posit a prime mover or first cause.

Buddhism Science (Physics & Neuroscience) Philosophy
Dependent origination (pratītya‑samutpāda): events arise with conditions; beginningless cycle; avoids eternalism and nihilism. Relational causality: systems evolve from prior states; Big Bang as initial condition, not metaphysical origin; networks have no single root node. Contrast: Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover; classical cosmological arguments posit a first cause; Madhyamaka denies inherent existence.
No‑self (anatta): person = aggregates; no core essence to begin with. Emergence: mind arises from neural interactions; memory from distributed traces; no “origin neuron.” Ontological neutrality: some philosophies adopt process metaphysics; others maintain substance ontology.
Practical import: change conditions (attention, ethics) → change mind. Intervention: change parameters (practice, therapy) → plasticity; change boundary conditions → different macrostates. Method: explanatory sufficiency without positing an ultimate starter.

Each circle represents a domain’s cycle: there is direction and dependency, but no privileged “first” link. Explanations begin from current conditions and trace relations.
